title: Given tasks with prerequisite dependencies, produce a valid order to complete them, or detect that no order exists because of a cycle, using topological sort.
shortTitle: Topological Sort and Cycle Detection (Course Schedule via Kahn's Algorithm)

s1_definition.profdef: A topological sort of a directed acyclic graph is a linear ordering of its nodes such that every directed edge points from an earlier node to a later node, meaning every prerequisite comes before the task that depends on it. Kahn's algorithm computes it by repeatedly removing nodes with zero remaining in-degree. If the graph has a cycle, no valid ordering exists, and Kahn's algorithm detects this because fewer than all nodes get emitted. It runs in time proportional to nodes plus edges.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India onboards a new product through a series of steps where some steps cannot start until others finish, for example "open ledger" must happen before "post opening balance." A planner writes each step on a card with arrows to the steps that depend on it. She first does all the steps that depend on nothing, then crosses off their arrows, which may free up new steps that now depend on nothing, and she does those next. She keeps going until every step is scheduled. If at some point steps remain but none are free, the steps are stuck waiting on each other in a circle, which means the plan is impossible.
s1_definition.oneliner: Repeatedly emit nodes with zero in-degree and decrement their neighbours; if you cannot emit all nodes, there is a cycle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A topological sort of a directed acyclic graph is a linear ordering of its nodes such that every directed edge points from an earlier node to a later node, meaning every prerequisite comes before the task that depends on it. Kahn's algorithm computes it by repeatedly removing nodes with zero remaining in-degree. If the graph has a cycle, no valid ordering exists, and Kahn's algorithm detects this because fewer than all nodes get emitted. It runs in time proportional to nodes plus edges.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India onboards a new product through a series of steps where some steps cannot start until others finish, for example "open ledger" must happen before "post opening balance." A planner writes each step on a card with arrows to the steps that depend on it. She first does all the steps that depend on nothing, then crosses off their arrows, which may free up new steps that now depend on nothing, and she does those next. She keeps going until every step is scheduled. If at some point steps remain but none are free, the steps are stuck waiting on each other in a circle, which means the plan is impossible.

**One line to remember:** Repeatedly emit nodes with zero in-degree and decrement their neighbours; if you cannot emit all nodes, there is a cycle.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem is modelled as a directed graph where an edge from A to B means A is a prerequisite of B. A valid completion order is a topological sort, which only exists if the graph is acyclic. Kahn's algorithm is the breadth-first approach and has the pleasant property of detecting cycles for free.

First you compute the in-degree of every node, which is the number of prerequisites it still has, and build an adjacency list of each node's dependents. You seed a queue with every node whose in-degree is zero, because those have no prerequisites and can start immediately. Then you loop: poll a node, append it to the order, and for each of its dependents decrement their in-degree; whenever a dependent's in-degree drops to zero, it is now free, so you enqueue it. For example `if (--inDegree[next] == 0) queue.offer(next);`.

The cycle check is elegant. If the graph is acyclic, every node eventually reaches in-degree zero and gets emitted, so the output has all n nodes. If there is a cycle, the nodes in the cycle permanently wait on each other, never reach in-degree zero, and never get emitted, so the output has fewer than n nodes. Comparing the emitted count to n tells you whether a valid order exists. The running time is nodes plus edges because each node is enqueued once and each edge is relaxed once.

A senior-level nuance is the alternative depth-first topological sort, which pushes nodes onto a stack after exploring all their descendants and detects cycles via a recursion-stack marker. I prefer Kahn's for its explicit in-degree model and natural cycle count, and I note the real-world uses: build systems ordering compilation, task schedulers resolving dependencies, Spring resolving bean creation order, and database migration tools ordering scripts. All of these are topological sort with cycle detection under the hood.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India onboards new products through dependent steps, and the workflow engine must compute a valid execution order so no step runs before its prerequisites. This is exactly a topological sort of the dependency graph.

Problem 2 — If someone misconfigures the dependencies so that two steps wait on each other, the workflow would deadlock forever. The engine must detect that cycle up front and refuse to start, rather than hang. Kahn's algorithm detects the cycle by emitting fewer than all steps.

In our mini-project we build an `OnboardingPlanner` that takes a number of steps and prerequisite pairs and returns a valid order, or flags a cycle. The demo runs one solvable workflow and logs the order.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: four steps and the prerequisite edges zero-before-one, zero-before-two, one-before-three, two-before-three.

Step 1: Build the graph. Step zero points to one and two. Step one points to three. Step two points to three. The in-degrees are: step zero zero, step one one, step two one, step three two.

Step 2: Seed the queue with zero-in-degree steps. Only step zero has no prerequisites, so the queue holds zero.

Step 3: Poll step zero, append it to the order. Decrement its dependents: step one drops from one to zero and step two drops from one to zero, so both are now free and get enqueued. The queue holds one then two.

Step 4: Poll step one, append it. Decrement its dependent step three from two to one, not yet free. The queue holds two.

Step 5: Poll step two, append it. Decrement step three from one to zero, now free, so enqueue it. The queue holds three.

Step 6: Poll step three, append it. It has no dependents. The queue is empty. The order has all four steps, so no cycle, and the valid order is zero, one, two, three. Each prerequisite correctly precedes its dependent.

```
[2026-10-26 23:31:01] INFO    Valid onboarding order: [0, 1, 2, 3]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A topological sort of a directed acyclic graph is a linear ordering of the nodes where every edge points from an earlier node to a later one, which means every prerequisite comes before the task that depends on it. A valid order only exists if the graph has no cycle. I use Kahn's algorithm, the breadth-first approach, because it computes the order and detects cycles in the same pass.

I start by computing each node's in-degree, which is how many prerequisites it still has, and I build an adjacency list of dependents. I seed a queue with every node whose in-degree is zero, since those can start immediately. Then I loop: I poll a node, append it to the order, and for each of its dependents I decrement the in-degree, and whenever a dependent reaches zero it becomes free and I enqueue it. The cycle check falls out naturally: if the graph is acyclic every node eventually reaches in-degree zero and gets emitted, so the output has all n nodes, but if there is a cycle the nodes in it wait on each other forever and never get emitted, so the output is short. Comparing the emitted count to n tells me whether a valid order exists, and the whole thing runs in nodes plus edges time.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the product-onboarding workflow engine, which runs dependent steps such as opening the ledger before posting the opening balance. The planner computes a valid execution order so no step runs before its prerequisites, and crucially it detects a misconfigured dependency cycle up front and refuses to start, instead of deadlocking forever at runtime.

The senior-level point I make is that there is a depth-first alternative that pushes nodes onto a stack after exploring all their descendants and detects cycles with a recursion-stack marker, but I prefer Kahn's for its explicit in-degree model and free cycle count. I also point out that this exact algorithm underpins build systems ordering compilation, task schedulers, Spring resolving bean creation order, and migration tools ordering scripts, so it is one of the most practically used graph algorithms in real software.
